## Overview and grading

### What you'll practice

In this graded assignment, you will practice with shell scripts,
running software with containers, rendering Markdown with Pandoc,
and version control with Git and GitHub.

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Oct 11^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: You will submit your assignment by tagging the instructors in an
  Issue in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.

::: {#oral-exam .callout-note}
#### Oral examination
For one of the three remaining graded assignments (this one, GA3, and GA4–GA5),
each of you will be asked to explain your work in a short oral examination.
You won't know in advance which assignment this will be.
We'll ask you to walk us through how you approached a few of the questions
and to explain your answers.

If you worked through the assignment yourself, there is nothing to worry about:
we just want to hear you talk through your reasoning.
It's completely fine if you've forgotten details of a command or concept,
even one you used correctly.
You'll only lose points for a question if it's clear that you really don't
understand your own answer to it.
If this is the case for several questions,
you may be asked to redo the assignment in the form of a replacement assignment.

We'll use 15-minute time slots for the oral examinations,
and we'll schedule them after the assignment deadline.
We'd also like to use a few minutes of this time to hear about your overall
experience with the course so far (this part is not graded).
:::

### GenAI check --- like previously, but with more details on expectations

This is the last graded assignment for which you are _not_ allowed to use
generative AI tools.
The guidelines are just like for the previous graded assignments,
but we provide some additional details on proper citation:

- You are allowed to search the internet, consult books, and so on,
  but you are **not** allowed to use generative AI tools.
  As such, using **Google AI Mode** output is not allowed either, but unfortunately,
  it may pop up even when you're trying to use Google for regular web searches.
  In case that helps, please note that one way to prevent AI mode output from
  showing up at all is adding `-ai` to your Google search queries.

- For any **unprompted use of commands, options, or other code we didn't cover in the course**,
  you must provide, **separately for each 'novel' use of code**, the **specific source**,
  where you quote the relevant lines that explain it.
  A general reference to a website or book that may explain 100s of commands/options/etc.

  Alternatively, you can argue you simply knew that command already,
  from previous self-study or experience.
  If you provide neither a source nor an explanation for commands not covered in
  the course, you will not earn any points for the relevant question(s).

### Part C: A script to run MultiQC

MultiQC is a very useful program that summarizes per-sample results of FastQC
and other bioinformatics programs into a single multi-sample report.
This allows you to easily compare results across multiple samples.

MultiQC takes a path to a **directory** as input,
and it will recursively search that directory for files that it can summarize,
such as FastQC results. It will then write its summary report to an output directory.

08. MultiQC isn't available as an OSC module (_optional_: verify this).
    Get a link from the Seqera Containers website to a **container** with the most
    recent version of MultiQC (`bioconda::multiqc` is the correct hit).

09. Print MultiQC's help info by running `multiqc --help` with your container link.
    Use the help info to figure out how to run MultiQC with `results/fastqc` as its
    input dir and `results/multiqc` as its output dir,
    and write down that command in your `README.md` (don't run it yet).

10. Write a script, `scripts/multiqc.sh`, to run MultiQC using the command you
    wrote above.
    That is, the script will have the input and output paths "hard-coded" in it.
    _Optional_: add some logging statements to the script with `echo`,
    like we did in class for the `fastqc.sh` script.

11. Run your script to summarize the FastQC results with MultiQC.
    MultiQC will print logging information to the screen ---
    how many FastQC reports does it say it found,
    and does that match what you expected?
    Commit your `scripts/multiqc.sh` script now that you know it works.

12. Change your `scripts/multiqc.sh` script so that it accepts
    **two arguments**, the input dir and the output dir,
    and uses these when running MultiQC.
    Then, rerun your script, passing the same input and output dirs as before
    (`results/fastqc` and `results/multiqc`) as arguments.
    Commit your updated script to Git,
    so your Git history will now contain both versions of the script.

13. Compare the second MultiQC run with the first one:
    do you notice any differences in what MultiQC printed to the screen,
    and in the names of the output files it created? What caused these differences?

### Part B: Basic shell scripts

<details><summary>**4.** Predict the output of `echo.sh`</summary>

1. `bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08` prints `Oct07` and `Oct08`,
   and then fails with an "unbound variable" error,
   because no third argument was passed,
   and `set -u` turns the use of an unset variable into an error.
   So, `Finished` is not printed.
2. `bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 Oct09 Oct10` prints `Oct07`, `Oct08`, `Oct09`,
   and `Finished`.
   The fourth argument is ignored, since the script never uses `$4`.
3. `bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 "Oct09 Oct10"` prints `Oct07`, `Oct08`,
   `Oct09 Oct10` (on one line), and `Finished`.
   The quotes make `Oct09 Oct10` a single argument.
4. In `bash scripts/echo.sh results/fastqc/*.html`,
   the shell expands the glob _before_ running the script,
   so the script receives 44 file paths as arguments.
   It prints the first three of these (in alphabetical order) and `Finished`.

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** Run `echo.sh` and compare with your predictions</summary>

```bash
bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08
```
```bash-out
Oct07
Oct08
scripts/echo.sh: line 6: $3: unbound variable
```

```bash
bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 Oct09 Oct10
```
```bash-out
Oct07
Oct08
Oct09
Finished
```

```bash
bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 "Oct09 Oct10"
```
```bash-out
Oct07
Oct08
Oct09 Oct10
Finished
```

```bash
bash scripts/echo.sh results/fastqc/*.html
```
```bash-out
results/fastqc/S63_R1_fastqc.html
results/fastqc/S63_R2_fastqc.html
results/fastqc/S64_R1_fastqc.html
Finished
```

See the answer to question 4 for an explanation of each output.

</details>

<details><summary>**6.** Write the `printline.sh` script</summary>

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/printline.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Copy the placeholder variables
input_file=$1
line_nr=$2

# Print the requested line
head -n "$line_nr" "$input_file" | tail -n 1
```

- `head -n "$line_nr"` prints all lines up to and including the requested one,
  and `tail -n 1` then keeps only the last of those lines.
- Other approaches, like `sed -n "${line_nr}p"` or `awk`, work too,
  but because we didn't cover these in class, you'd need to provide a source.

</details>

<details><summary>**7.** Test `printline.sh` twice</summary>

```bash
bash scripts/printline.sh data/metadata.tsv 1
```
```bash-out
sample_id	time	treatment
```

```bash
bash scripts/printline.sh data/metadata.tsv 5 > results/metadata_line5.txt
cat results/metadata_line5.txt
```
```bash-out
S83	10dpi	cathemerium
```

</details>

### Part C: A script to run MultiQC

<details><summary>**8.** Get a MultiQC container link</summary>

_Optional_: check that MultiQC isn't available as an OSC module:

```bash
module spider multiqc
```
```bash-out
# TODO: paste output from OSC
```

The container link (URI) for the most recent version of MultiQC (1.35) is:

```bash-in-nocolor
oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc:1.35--562c547b518ebe20
```

Make sure to use the `oras://` URI rather than the Docker one.

</details>

<details><summary>**9.** MultiQC's help info, and the MultiQC command</summary>

```bash
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc:1.35--562c547b518ebe20 \
    multiqc --help
```

The relevant line of the output:

```bash-out
│ --outdir           -o  Create report in the specified output directory. (TEXT)                                                   │
```

And the usage line, `multiqc [OPTIONS] [ANALYSIS DIRECTORY]`,
shows that the input dir is passed as an argument.
So, the MultiQC command is:

```bash
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc:1.35--562c547b518ebe20 \
    multiqc --outdir results/multiqc results/fastqc
```

Using `-o` instead of `--outdir` is fine too.

</details>

<details><summary>**10.** Write the `multiqc.sh` script</summary>

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/multiqc.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run MultiQC
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc:1.35--562c547b518ebe20 \
    multiqc --outdir results/multiqc results/fastqc
```

As for the _optional_ logging statements, you could for example add
`echo "Starting script multiqc.sh"` and `date` lines at the start and end of the script,
like in the `fastqc.sh` script from class.

</details>

<details><summary>**11.** Run `multiqc.sh`</summary>

```bash
bash scripts/multiqc.sh
```

The relevant lines of the output:

```bash-out
       file_search | Search path: /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/GA3/results/fastqc
            fastqc | Found 44 reports
     write_results | Data        : results/multiqc/multiqc_data
     write_results | Report      : results/multiqc/multiqc_report.html
           multiqc | MultiQC complete
```

- MultiQC found **44 reports**.
  This is as expected, because FastQC ran once for each of the 44 FASTQ files
  (22 samples × R1 and R2).
- If you ran FastQC on fewer files in class, you'll see a lower number,
  which is fine as long as you can explain it.
- Commit the script once you've seen that it works.

</details>

<details><summary>**12.** Make `multiqc.sh` accept arguments, and rerun it</summary>

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/multiqc.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Copy the placeholder variables
indir=$1
outdir=$2

# Run MultiQC
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc:1.35--562c547b518ebe20 \
    multiqc --outdir "$outdir" "$indir"
```

```bash
bash scripts/multiqc.sh results/fastqc results/multiqc
```

Then, commit the updated script,
so your Git history contains both versions of the script.

</details>

<details><summary>**13.** Differences between the two MultiQC runs</summary>

In the second run, MultiQC printed the following line:

```bash-out
Existing reports found, adding suffix to filenames. Use '--force' to overwrite.
```

So, rather than overwriting the output files from the first run,
it added a `_1` suffix to the names of the new output files.
The output dir now contains both reports:

```bash
ls results/multiqc
```
```bash-out
multiqc_data  multiqc_data_1  multiqc_report_1.html  multiqc_report.html
```

- These differences are caused by using the same output dir twice,
  combined with MultiQC not overwriting existing reports by default.
  The `--force` (`-f`) option would make it overwrite them.
- The change to the script did _not_ cause the differences,
  because the MultiQC command that the script runs is the same as before.

</details>

### Part D: Pandoc to render Markdown

<details><summary>**14.** The structure of the Pandoc command</summary>

In `pandoc -o README.pdf README.md`:

- `pandoc` is the command (program).
- `-o README.pdf` is an **option** that takes a value, the output file
  (`-o` is short for `--output`).
- `README.md` is an **argument**, the input file.

Pandoc infers the output format from the **extension of the output file name**
(`.pdf`),
and similarly, the input format from the extension of the input file name (`.md`).
You can also set the formats explicitly with the `--to` (`-t`) and `--from` (`-f`) options.

</details>

<details><summary>**15.** Render your README to PDF and HTML</summary>

```bash
pandoc -o README.pdf README.md
ls -lh README.pdf
```
```bash-out
# TODO: paste output from OSC
```

Following from the answer to question 14,
you only need to change the output file's extension to render to HTML:

```bash
pandoc -o README.html README.md
```

</details>

<details><summary>**16.** Should the rendered files be committed?</summary>

- Generally, **no**: the PDF and HTML files are output that you can regenerate
  from `README.md` at any time, just like the files in `results`.
  Committing them would add redundant files to your repo,
  and each time you change your README,
  you'd also need to rerender and commit these files to keep them in sync.
  Also, Git can't show meaningful differences between versions of a binary file like a PDF.
- You could add these files to your `.gitignore`,
  e.g. with the lines `README.pdf` and `README.html`.
- That said, a "yes" with a reasonable justification is also fine ---
  for example, to make the PDF directly available to collaborators
  who don't use Markdown.

</details>

### Part E: Publish your repo on GitHub

<details><summary>**18--20.** Create a GitHub repo, push, and create an Issue</summary>

After creating the repo on GitHub:

```bash
git remote add origin git@github.com:<github-username>/GA3.git
git push -u origin main
```

- Your GitHub repo should be public,
  or you should have added `kstarr791` and `jelmerp` as collaborators.
- Your GitHub repo should contain your final `README.md`, `.gitignore`, and `scripts`,
  but not `data` or `results`.
- Your Issue should tag `@kstarr791` and `@jelmerp` in its text box.

</details>
